Beállítom Csütörtök reggel fekete füst szállt fel az oroszországi Jaroszlavl városban, amelyet az ukrán hadsereg az éjjel több száz drónnal támadott. A BBC azt írja, ebben a városban található Oroszország egyik legnagyobb kőolaj-finomítója, amelyet Ukrajna több alkalommal is célba vett az elmúlt hónapokban. Volodimir Zelenszkij ukrán elnök azt közölte, ezen kívül egy másik orosz finomítót is támadtak. Az orosz védelmi minisztérium közlése szerint az éjjeli támadás során 605 ukrán drónt semmisített meg a légvédelem. Ez az összesített szám több területre vonatkozik, ahol támadások történtek, beleértve Moszkva környékét, a Fekete-tengeri régiót, valamint a finomítónak is otthont adó Jaroszlavlt. A jaroszlavli finomító csaknem 700 kilométerre fekszik az orosz–ukrán határtól. Nagyjából 3500 ember dolgozik az 1961-ben épült üzemben, és évente mintegy 15 millió tonna olajat képes termelni. Csütörtökön az ukrán hadsereg egy másik finomítót is támadott, amely Baskíriában található. Az ukrán csapások után Oroszország négy rakétával és több mint 100 drónnal hajtott végre csapásokat Ukrajna területén, mintegy 18 helyszínen jelentettek károkat. A délelőtti hírek szerint az orosz támadások még nem értek véget. Az ukrán Harkiv városát ért csapások a hatóságok szerint két ember halálát okozták, és legalább nyolcan megsérültek, miután az oroszok egy vasútállomást támadtak. https://www.dailysabah.com/politics/3-in.text: Politics Diplomacy Legislation War On Terror EU Affairs Elections News Analysis 3 injured after drone strike hits Turkish cargo ship in Black Sea by Daily Sabah ISTANBUL Aug 03, 2026 - 9:08 pm GMT+3 Edited By Nurbanu Tanrıkulu Kızıl by Daily Sabah Aug 03, 2026 9:08 pm Edited By Nurbanu Tanrıkulu Kızıl Three crew members were critically injured after a Turkish-owned roll-on/roll-off (Ro-Ro) cargo ship came under a drone attack in the Black Sea on Monday, Turkish maritime authorities said. The NADEZHDA, a Turkish-owned cargo vessel sailing from Russia's Novorossiysk to the Turkish port of Samsun, was attacked about 20 nautical miles (37 kilometers) off Novorossiysk on Monday, according to a statement by Türkiye's Directorate General of Maritime Affairs. The vessel was carrying 22 crew members, including 13 Turkish nationals. Initial assessments indicated the ship sustained damage to its living quarters and bow, while a fire continued to burn on board. The Directorate General of Maritime Affairs said that, following coordination with Russia's Maritime Rescue Coordination Center (MRCC) in Novorossiysk, all crew members were safely evacuated to the Russian port by Russian maritime units. According to preliminary information cited in the statement, three crew members may have sustained critical injuries. The agency added that the fire remained active aboard the vessel, but rescue operations could not be carried out because of the continuing risk of drone attacks in the area. The Directorate General of Maritime Affairs said it was closely monitoring the situation and wished all affected seafarers a speedy recovery and safe return to their families. More than three years of the Russia-Ukraine war have jeopardized maritime security in the Black Sea. Türkiye has witnessed several drones of Russian or Ukrainian origin crash on its territory, while uncrewed armed naval vessels have frequently washed ashore. In response to growing threats, Türkiye, Romania and Bulgaria established a maritime security initiative primarily tasked with clearing stray naval mines in the Black Sea. shortlink copied Last Update: Aug 03, 2026 10:39 pm KEYWORDS drone attacks ukraine türkiye black sea novorossiysk russia samsun The Daily Sabah Newsletter Keep up to date with what’s happening in Turkey, it’s region and the world. https://www.dw.com/en/germany-s-goethe-i.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MOSm The Goethe-Institut in Moscow is one of three branches of Germany’s cultural center that'll have to close Image: Ramil Sitdikov/REUTERS Advertisement Germany's Goethe-Institut will close all Russian branches by September 13 amid one of the worst spats in the history of relations between Russia and Germany . The Russian foreign ministry ordered the closure of the German cultural centers in Moscow , St. Petersburg and Novosibirsk in response to Berlin's reaction to the attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport in early August. The German authorities blamed Moscow for organizing the attack and announced sanctions. They include closing the Russian culture and education center in Berlin, known as the Russian House , and the Russian Consulate General in Bonn, as well tightening visa restrictions for Russian citizens. "All employees must cease their work in Russia as of September 13, 2026," Secretary General of the Goethe-Institut Gitte Zschoch said in a statement. "No more books can be borrowed from our libraries, and no further training can be offered. German language teachers are losing an important source of professional training and support. For people in Russia, this further restricts access to the German language, culture and reliable information from and about Germany." The library of the Goethe-Institut's Moscow branch won't be accessible anymore after September 13 either Image: Timur Gusarov/TASS/picture alliance DW asked its users in Russia to share how the closure of the Goethe-Institut will affect them personally. The responses received do not constitute a representative survey. All users shared their stories on conditions of anonymity. Russian authorities labeled DW an "undesirable organization" making every cooperation with the media company a criminal offense. 'We'll have to travel to another country' for German exams Many DW readers fear that, after the closure of the Goethe-Institut branches, they or their relatives will no longer be able to take exams in Russia for internationally recognized German language certificates. Some readers pointed out that closing the Goethe-Institut in Russia will hit ethnic Germans willing to relocate back to Germany, or late repatriates, especially hard. "I no longer live in Russia, having emigrated as a late repatriate, but my parents are still in Russia and were planning to take exams at the Goethe-Institut this fall or winter before submitting their resettlement documents. It looks like they'll have to take the exams in another country, which means additional stress and expenses for them," one reader said. DW also received responses from parents whose children are learning German and plan to continue their education in Germany. "My son attends a German school, and now we won't be able to take the exam in Russia. We'll have to travel to another country," one message said. Germany blames Russia for attempted terror attack in Leipzig To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video It remains unclear whether exams, language courses and educational programs will continue in Russia in another format or through partner organizations. Several readers expressed hope that at least some services will remain available online. Goethe-Institute closures hit teachers hard The closure of the institute will affect not only those planning to move to Germany or enroll at a German university. A German language teacher from the Moscow region told DW that her school had cooperated with the Goethe-Institut for more than 15 years. "This partnership was one of the most important pillars of our work. The institute supported us with high-quality teaching materials and provided modern books and publications about life in Germany, helping us make lessons engaging and relevant. Our students attended additional courses, and many successfully passed the Goethe certificate exams," she wrote. "I teach German and can't find a job in Russia," another teacher told DW. "It's terrible. I'm a German teacher, and I feel professionally stranded and lost," a third wrote. Despite the restrictions imposed since the beginning of Russia's war in Ukraine in 2022, demand for the institute's services remained high. According to the Goethe-Institut, around 10,000 people studied German through its programs and partnerships in 2025. Before 2023, that number used to stand at around 16,000 people. The institute administered roughly 22,000 exams, and its libraries were visited by 6,700 people in 2025. 'Culture has become a hostage to political decisions' Many readers perceive what is happening as another stage in the destruction of ties between Russia and Germany. "We would like cultural relations between the Russian Federation and Germany not to be destroyed," one DW user responded. "It is sad to realize that culture has become a hostage to political decisions. The closure of the Goethe-Institut will affect people who have no way of influencing politicians." Leipzig/Halle airport in Germany was the target of an attempted drone attack in August 2026 Image: Axel Schmidt/REUTERS Some DW readers from Russia specifically draw attention to the responsibility of politicians. One reader called the decision to close the institutes another step toward isolating the country and wondered why its consequences affect ordinary citizens rather than the Russian politicians who make such decisions. "Why can the people making decisions to isolate Russia from Europe simultaneously provide their own children and close relatives with a European education and a European way of life?" a DW user asked, proposing a ban on the education of the children and close relatives of members of Russia's top leadership at universities in Germany and other EU countries. Part of the audience considers Moscow's decision expected. "The closure of the branches looks like a logical response to the closure of the Russian House in Germany. Could it have been otherwise? It is a pity that cultural and humanitarian ties between the countries are becoming hostages to politics," one reader wrote. Some Russians hold Germany responsible for deteriorating relationship Some Russians however believe that closing the Goethe-Institut branches in Russia was the right step and blame Germany for the recent escalation of the conflict with Russia. "German authorities have buried cultural cooperation with Russia by shutting down the Russian House. The responsibility lies entirely with the German side, " said one of the survey participants. A bilateral intergovernmental agreement between Russia and Germany from 2011 regulates the work of the Russian House in Berlin and the Goethe-Institut's branches in Russia. It obliges both countries, on the basis of reciprocity, to ensure conditions necessary for the operation of their cultural centers. However, it does not in any way provide for the automatic closure of one country's cultural centers in response to the other country doing so. President of the Goethe-Institut Gesche Joost called the closure of its branches in Russia "the end of an era in German-Russian cultural relations." According to its website, the Goethe-Institut has 154 branches in 100 countries. This number includes the three branches in Russia that are now being closed. https://www.mfa.gov.lv/en/article/talks-.text: In talks with EU Member State ambassadors, the Foreign Minister highlights Latvia’s interests in the next EU Multiannual Financial Framework Published: 16.10.2026. Flickr Photo: Laura Celmiņa, Ministry of Foreign Affairs Facebook X / Twitter Linkedin Threads On 15 October 2026, Minister of Foreign Affairs Baiba Braže met with the ambassadors of the European Union (EU) Member States to Latvia. During the meeting, Irish Ambassador to Latvia Marcella Smyth outlined the priorities of the Irish Presidency of the Council of the EU, whilst Baiba Braže highlighted Latvia’s interests in the next EU Multiannual Financial Framework. The Minister for Foreign Affairs expressed her support for the priorities set out by the Irish Presidency and highlighted the EU issues of greatest importance to Latvia – strengthening Latvia’s eastern border, continuing support for Ukraine, strengthening the EU’s security and defence capabilities, and protecting Latvia’s interests in negotiations on the EU Multiannual Financial Framework. Speaking about the negotiations on the EU Multiannual Financial Framework for 2028–2034, the Minister highlighted Latvia’s key priorities – adequate funding for security and defence, additional funding for Latvia as an EU Member State on the EU’s eastern border, the equalisation of direct payments, and funding for EU connectivity and military mobility, including the implementation of the Rail Baltica project. During the discussions, the Minister expressed her support for efforts to strengthen EU’s competitiveness, tying this to the priority of security. It is important that, whilst developing Europe’s economic and industrial potential, targeted investment is ensured in innovation, digital development and the defence industry. The Minister of Foreign Affairs also noted that Latvia supports opening all negotiating clusters for EU accession with Ukraine and Moldova as soon as possible.
